First, we compute ${D}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}^{2} & =D\cdot D \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{4} \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{4} \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{4} \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =D\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that ${D}^{2}=D,$ so $D$ is an idempotent matrix.

We can use this fact to compute ${D}^{3}$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}^{3} & ={D}^{2}\cdot D \\  & =D\cdot D \\  & ={D}^{2} \\  & =D\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{D}^{3}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{4} \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}].
$$
